title: 4 ways to address the failures we found along the US border’s “virtual wall”
gist: MIT Technology Review sets out four fixes for the US border surveillance network after finding more than 1,050 migrant deaths near towers: audit deaths near the towers, repair migrant-death record keeping, actually measure when technology leads to an apprehension, and treat each death near a tower as a potential surveillance failure. The piece documents that CBP has never run such an audit despite having the internal data since at least 2015, while the US prepares to spend $1 billion tripling the network by 2034.

insights.claim: The US is set to spend $1 billion to triple the size of its border surveillance tower network by 2034, while no comprehensive assessment of how many people have died near the existing towers has ever been conducted.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Spending scales while the evidence base does not — the mismatch is the political risk that could eventually reprice these contracts.
insights.quote: The US is set to spend $1 billion to triple the size of the virtual wall by 2034.
insights.locator: Each of these deaths should have raised alarms

insights.claim: CBP has been able to audit tower effectiveness and quantify deaths near them since at least 2015, when it began installing the tower types analyzed, but sources say it has never done so.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Capability without action is the strongest evidence that non-measurement is a choice rather than a data limitation.
insights.locator: An internal audit would not have such limitations

insights.claim: CBP does not publish a comprehensive map of its surveillance towers, forcing outside analysts to rely on the Electronic Frontier Foundation's mapping plus satellite verification and leaving them with nearly 600 towers against the roughly 800 the government says operate today.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Roughly a quarter of the installed base is outside public view, so every external estimate of program performance is structurally incomplete.

insights.claim: The tally of more than 1,050 deaths near towers is explicitly an undercount because the tower catalog is incomplete and installation dates are inexact, leaving no complete picture of where along the border the problem is worst.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Treat the published figure as a floor; an internal audit would likely raise it, which matters for the severity of any eventual political response.
insights.quote: That means our tally of more than 1,050 people who have died near them is an undercount.

insights.claim: No national agency collects and publishes all available records on migrant deaths, and there is no shared protocol for documenting them in public records, which is why even an exhaustive review of dozens of Texas agencies yields an incomplete picture.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: The absent data layer is a prerequisite for any effectiveness analysis; until it exists, program evaluation is impossible by construction.
insights.locator: If CBP is to analyze instances where people have died

insights.claim: Border Patrol has run an internal death-tracking system since 2007, but national rules for how sectors enter cases were only established in 2021, and the GAO found the following year that many cases still were not tracked, especially deaths not discovered by Border Patrol itself.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Fourteen years between system launch and entry standards explains why official death counts are consistently below outside estimates.
insights.locator: Border Patrol has had its own internal system

insights.claim: The Missing Migrant Program launched in 2017 was found by the GAO in April 2025 to be improving data collection on 911 calls and rescues but to have no plan for using that data to measure whether it actually increases rescues or reduces deaths — its two primary goals — and neither GAO recommendation has been implemented.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: A program that collects outcome data but refuses to compute outcomes is the clearest single illustration of the measurement vacuum.
insights.locator: In addition to tracking migrant deaths

insights.claim: After CBP agreed in 2014 to log when technology aided an apprehension, the GAO reported in 2017 that the data was inaccurate and unreliable, finding agents in Texas who credited a specific type of tower hundreds of times even though no such towers existed anywhere in the state.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Attribution data this corrupted cannot support any vendor-level efficacy claim, in either direction.
insights.quote: it found agents in Texas, for example, who were crediting a specific type of tower in apprehensions hundreds of times, even though no such towers existed anywhere in the state
insights.locator: Then, in 2017, the GAO reported that the data being collected was inaccurate

insights.claim: More than seven years after agreeing to assess the towers' effectiveness, CBP still had not produced any analysis by August 2021; it finished one in 2022 but the results are not public, so the network is growing faster than anyone is assessing its impact.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: The one completed internal assessment being withheld is a meaningful signal about what it likely found.
insights.quote: That means the virtual wall is growing faster than anyone is assessing its impact.
insights.locator: And in August 2021, more than seven years after it agreed

insights.claim: Frontline agents still treat technology-assist logging as a low priority despite repeated commitments to train them, with one former CBP official calling the mandate 'spitting in the wind' because the messy reality of apprehensions does not translate into neat metrics.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Metric collection that conflicts with frontline incentives will not survive contact with operations — a general lesson for outcome-based procurement.
insights.quote: spitting in the wind, to be honest
insights.locator: Border Patrol again said it would improve

insights.claim: There is no requirement and no process for Border Patrol agents who find a body to check whether the person died near surveillance infrastructure, so migrant deaths are never routinely treated as possible failures of the surveillance network.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Without a failure-classification step, no amount of new sensor spending can be validated or invalidated by outcomes.
insights.locator: Several agents and officials told us that if Border Patrol agents

insights.claim: CBP typically deletes tower surveillance footage after 30 days unless an internal review is opened, which usually happens only for deaths in custody, so flagging deaths near towers would at minimum preserve footage for investigators and families.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: A 30-day retention window is a low-cost, high-leverage policy change and the most likely concrete reform to emerge from this reporting.
insights.quote: CBP typically deletes surveillance footage from the towers after 30 days unless an internal review is opened, which usually happens only for deaths in custody.
insights.locator: Without that check, law enforcement, medical investigators

insights.claim: Agents already log GPS coordinates when they apprehend a group or encounter footprints, so automatically cross-checking every migrant death against CBP's internal tower database would require no new data collection — only the will to run the query.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: The audit is cheap and technically trivial, which means continued absence is a governance decision rather than a resource constraint.
insights.locator: CBP should automatically check every migrant death

insights.claim: At one New Mexico location several people died within a few months of each other, sometimes just hundreds of feet apart, in clear sight of an advanced AI tower — a cluster that a routine postmortem review would flag as either repeated camera detection failure or repeated non-response by agents.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Spatial clustering makes tower-level defect detection straightforward; its absence from agency practice is the accountability gap in one example.
insights.locator: Consider one location we identified in New Mexico

insights.claim: A New Mexico state representative shown that more than 18 people died near surveillance towers in a single stretch of desert near her district in 2024 alone responded that the federal government should audit the program because it feels like it is not working.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: State-level political reaction to the data is the earliest indicator of whether federal scrutiny follows.
insights.quote: If I were the federal government, I would do an audit, because this feels like it’s not working.
insights.locator: 1. Conduct a comprehensive audit of deaths near the virtual wall
